#541. The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."

The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

This article was originally written in German.

#539. This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death. Instead, its extraordinary shape was completely natural and may represent the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a mammal.

Sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals. While most vertebrates have bodies and skulls that are roughly symmetrical on both sides, toothed whales have evolved uneven skull structures to accommodate specialized organs responsible for producing sound and navigating through echolocation.

Now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level. Named Scaphokogia huachafo, the whale lived during the Late Miocene, between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago, and measured approximately 2.7 meters in length. Its fossilized skull displays the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any whale or dolphin, and possibly in any mammal.

A Prehistoric Whale With an Extraordinary Skull

"Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked," explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study.

Benites-Palomino investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich's Department of Paleontology. He is currently an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale's extraordinary appearance also inspired its scientific name. The word huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and is commonly used to describe something excessively flashy, bizarre, extravagant, or even tacky.

"In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically," says Benites-Palomino.

"When we looked at the proportions of this whale - with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout - it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it."

Scientists Initially Suspected the Skull Was Deformed

The remarkable fossil was originally recovered during the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru. This desert region is famous among paleontologists for its exceptionally preserved fossils of ancient marine animals.

Benites-Palomino first encountered the specimen in 2015 while preparing his Bachelor's thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its dramatically uneven shape immediately raised an important question: Was the skull genuinely this crooked when the whale was alive, or had millions of years of geological pressure distorted it?

"The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy - that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years," says Benites-Palomino.

"But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation."

The findings confirmed that the extraordinary asymmetry was part of the whale's natural anatomy, rather than damage caused by burial, fossilization, or disease.

A Bizarre Adaptation for Hunting Along the Seafloor

The whale's unusual skull also offers clues about how it survived. Modern sperm whales typically pursue squid in deep ocean waters, but Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have followed a very different hunting strategy. Its anatomy suggests that it was highly adapted to searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal waters.

One of its most distinctive features was a large, tube-shaped snout strengthened by dense bone and cartilage that had hardened into bone. These heavy structures served as natural ballast, moving the whale's center of gravity forward and downward.

Its snout also pointed downward at an angle of 31 degrees relative to the rest of its skull. By reconstructing the joint connecting the skull to the first neck vertebra, known as the atlas, scientists determined that Scaphokogia could bend its head downward by as much as 55 degrees.

"The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom," explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, co-author of the study and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich.

"The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment."

Researchers also believe the whale may have relied on its highly specialized echolocation system to locate prey beneath the soft sediment of coastal environments. Unlike other marine mammals that forage along the ocean floor, Scaphokogia lacked the sensitive facial whiskers or specialized visual adaptations that can help animals find food near the bottom.

Instead, its extraordinarily asymmetrical skull may have supported a sophisticated biological sonar system that allowed it to detect hidden prey.

This unusual feeding strategy represents a specialized way of life that no longer exists among modern marine mammals. As ocean conditions shifted toward the end of the Miocene, the ecological niche occupied by Scaphokogia disappeared, eventually giving way to the marine mammal communities familiar today.

The discovery provides a remarkable glimpse into how far evolution once pushed the anatomy of whales, producing a creature whose dramatically crooked face was not a deformity, but an adaptation to a vanished underwater world.

Materials provided by University of Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#537. A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal. A new study published in Nature dates the ancient remains to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that the human family tree in southern Africa was much more complicated than previously believed.

The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB). The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how early human relatives evolved and how different species were related.

First discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity. It also became the original "type specimen" used to define the species Australopithecus africanus. However, scientists never established definitive criteria for assigning later fossil discoveries to this species. As a result, the Taung Child remains the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as Australopithecus africanus.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," says Professor Gabriele Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk -- it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts."

Ancient Fossils Reveal a More Complex Human Family Tree

To investigate how the Taung Child compared with other early human relatives, researchers examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth. They found that several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus followed developmental patterns that differed from those of the Taung Child.

Differences in brain development were particularly revealing. They suggest that fossils previously grouped into a single species may actually represent several distinct hominin species that inhabited the Sterkfontein region, either at the same time or during different periods.

These findings raise important questions about the diversity of our ancient ancestors and suggest that early human evolution followed a much more complicated path than scientists once assumed.

How Climate Change Shaped Human Evolution

The researchers believe that dramatic environmental changes played a major role in creating this evolutionary diversity. Millions of years ago, southern Africa experienced repeated shifts between wetter and drier climates, continually transforming the landscape and the habitats available to early human relatives.

As suitable environments expanded and contracted, ancient hominin populations moved with them. Some groups became geographically isolated and evolved along different paths, while others eventually came back into contact and interbred. These changing conditions also exposed populations to different predators and pathogens, creating additional pressures that shaped their evolution.

Southern Africa's position along the boundary between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it especially important in this process. Over thousands of years, shifting habitats may have repeatedly brought different hominin species together, creating opportunities for interbreeding and hybridization.

A Greener South Africa 3 Million Years Ago

The study also reveals a surprising picture of the environment in which the Taung Child lived. Evidence preserved in fossilized pollen indicates that the region was once considerably wetter and more heavily forested than it is today.

Researchers identified evidence of tree species that are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast, suggesting that the landscape surrounding the Taung Child was dramatically different from modern South Africa.

Together, these discoveries challenge the traditional view of human evolution as a relatively straightforward progression from one species to another. Instead, they point to a shifting network of populations that repeatedly separated, adapted, reunited, and sometimes interbred as environmental conditions changed.

More than 100 years after its discovery, the Taung Child is once again transforming our understanding of human origins. Its latest secrets suggest that the emergence of our own genus, Homo, was preceded by a far more diverse and interconnected world of ancient human relatives than previously recognized.

Materials provided by Vrije Universiteit Brussel. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#536. Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly

Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.

Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.

“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.

Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

This investigation was produced in partnership with Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom covering AI.

An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

In January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake with a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.

Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.

According to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.

“We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”

One ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.

ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”

“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek said in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.

Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions—a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.

The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof New and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic issues within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.

“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”

Like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post and accept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses said affects their ability to get shifts; and it offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, and dynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the company’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.

After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.

In court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree said it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lewis’ family.

A representative for Peachtree Centre declined to comment citing pending litigation. In court, the home pointed out Lewis was admitted to the hospital with many conditions besides effects from the injection, and her death certificate lists “senile degeneration of the brain” as the cause.

As part of the case, Kaye testified that she drove more than 250 miles from Myrtle Beach to work the Peachtree overnight shift. She had over two years of experience at the time and said she wasn’t given so much as a tour before being the only nurse posted to oversee a floor of 22 patients.

“This particular shift I had a lot of patients,” she testified in the August deposition. “It was very overwhelming.”

In their complaint against Peachtree and ShiftKey, Lewis’ family said they’d entrusted their “vulnerable” mother to a home they expected to “properly train staff.”

“I’ll never get Mom back,” said Lewis’ son, James Lewis, in a deposition earlier this year. “I just don't want it to happen to anybody else.”

Kara Smith can’t tell you where she’ll be working next week. A certified nursing assistant, Smith logs into the ShiftKey app most mornings to browse eight-hour shifts at more than a dozen long-term care facilities within driving distance from her West Virginia home.

Lured by the promise of scheduling freedom and premium pay for hard-to-fill shifts, Smith became a ShiftKey contractor in 2022. She claims she soon learned it's not unheard of to work night shifts at nursing homes staffed entirely by ShiftKey.

Founded in 2016 in Texas, ShiftKey grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as unprepared nursing homes reeled from rolling outbreaks that could claim dozens of lives in a single facility. Health care workers sought higher pay as their risks mounted, and homes scrambled to fill shifts.

Backed by private equity, ShiftKey and its competitors Clipboard Health and IntelyCare benefited. According to an analysis by the US Department of Health and Human Services, from 2019 to 2022, the use of contract staff in nursing homes tripled from 4 to 12 percent of all nursing hours. Though it’s since declined, the rate remains higher than prepandemic.

In 2023, ShiftKey’s then CEO told Axios that the company was valued at more than $2 billion.

Nursing homes pay ShiftKey set rates for workers. The platform then “mathematically” calculates a “suggested” rate for each shift posted, Vitek said in a statement, emphasizing that dynamic pricing tools are only used to increase pay for “difficult-to-fill” shifts—and never to decrease rates.

Workers then bid to claim it. This bidding system is what got Smith hooked: Instead of accepting whatever wage a facility would offer, Smith haggled for higher pay.

“If I can even make 25 extra cents, I'm going to try to push for that,” said Smith, a 47-year-old single mom. “Every penny counts.”

Since the pandemic, however, wages on ShiftKey have plummeted, according to several nurses who spoke with Proof News and WIRED. Teresa, an LPN who declined to give her last name, joined ShiftKey in 2019. She stopped using the platform last year when she noticed competition for shifts growing—and pay rates declining.

“People were fighting over trash shifts for under $20 an hour,” said Teresa, a single mother of three kids.

Smith remembers being able to bid $3 to $4 more an hour above the facility’s suggested rate when she first joined, but this year she said she’s been forced to accept less money or risk no work at all.

According to her ShiftKey payment records that she shared with Proof News and Wired, one facility paid her $32.50 an hour in the summer of 2025 and around $26 a year later. Payments from another nursing home showed the same downward trend. On Facebook groups, many ShiftKey workers have posted about a similar dip in earnings.

“The starting bids are shamefully low,” said Smith. “It’s not worth the workload or the drive.”

During her four years with ShiftKey, Smith said she routinely felt “thrown in” at new facilities without orientation, clear instructions, or logins. She said she had to work hard to familiarize herself with the residents’ conditions, because critical details, such as who is a fall risk or who has a catheter or an ostomy, are frequently missing. Hours in, she felt like she was in “an ocean and nobody’s around me.”

“We're coming there because they're short-handed,” said Smith. “So we are automatically going to be walking into a shit show.”

Smith said a lack of orientation led to scary close calls. Last year, she says she arrived at a Virginia nursing home with no advance information, not even the door code. She didn’t know anything about the patients, and that made her “very stressed out.”

“I know my blood pressure went up because of it,” she said.

Another time, Smith said she dropped off a regular drink to a resident only to later learn that they were prescribed only thickened liquids to avoid choking.

“What if they choked and died?” said Smith.

Facilities on ShiftKey have the option to require that workers attend a paid “orientation shift” before picking up a regular one. But four ShiftKey workers told Proof News and WIRED that they've frequently picked up nursing home shifts without doing an orientation shift first.

Inspection reports from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services dating back to 2023 and obtained by Proof News and WIRED reveal ShiftKey workers making dangerous mistakes.

In Ohio, after a ShiftKey nurse made a PICC line mistake at Stellar Care Center, a federal inspection report noted that the nursing home’s administrators had never checked to see whether she was trained to do IV therapy.

The report noted that an administrator had spoken with someone at ShiftKey, who told her that because they consider everyone on the app an independent contractor, the company didn’t test for what skills they knew.

In other cases, the orientation was inadequate. At Woodway Rehabilitation and Healthcare Center in Texas, a federal health surveyor spotted a ShiftKey worker trying to force-feed a resident a health shake using an oral syringe. The ShiftKey worker said it was her first time at the facility, according to the 2025 inspection report. She received some orientation for the facility on the app before she started her shift, the report said, but couldn’t remember if feeding was included.

In 2024, another CMS surveyor wrote that a ShiftKey nurse at the Medical Suites at Oak Creek in Wisconsin told the surveyor she was not shown any care plans for residents on her first day. According to the report, the surveyor spoke with an administrator, who handed the surveyor an undated orientation checklist. The administrator said they did not currently have a policy regarding orientation for gig nurses, but that she'd be implementing one in 30 minutes.

Neither Stellar Care, Woodway Rehab, nor the Medical Suites at Oak Creek responded to requests for comment on this story.

Researchers warn that gig nurses who aren’t properly oriented and who move constantly between facilities can disrupt the continuity of care. Jasmine Travers Altizer, an assistant professor at New York University’s Rory Meyers College of Nursing, conducted a qualitative study of 22 nursing home administrators this year and found that they felt relying on temporary workers led to “less consistent care, more hospital transfers, potentially unnecessary treatments and antibiotic use, and increased falls.” Administrators also reported staff having less ability to support one another across the facility.

Gig nursing “shouldn't be a fix for chronic understaffing,” said Travers Altizer in an email. It's critical, she said, to “have consistent staff who know the residents.”

In response, Vitek, the ShiftKey CEO, said, “Continuity of care is an important consideration in nursing home quality, but the issue predates platforms like ours.”

ShiftKey says its model keeps more nurses on the job during a time of critical shortage. Vitek said a survey of workers on ShiftKey found that more than a third stated they would not be able to stay in the health care industry without such a platform.

“We reject the premise that enabling independent flexible nursing support is harmful to the industry, because the challenge in addressing these issues is not about the choice between full-time staff versus temporary shift support,” he said.

Katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, said a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”

According to CMS data, the average time worked by nursing staff per resident at Peachtree, where Lewis was accidentally injected, is lower than the state average and less than minimum requirements set by the US Department of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration that are no longer in effect. The American Health Care Association, a nonprofit group that represents nursing homes, successfully challenged the rule in court in 2025, and the Trump administration ultimately withdrew the rule, stating that the move would save nursing homes $55.1 billion over the course of 10 years.

“We need to have minimum safe staffing levels,” said Hannah Garden-Monheit, who worked on nursing home reform at the White House National Economic Council and now is executive director of Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy. “The patients need that continuity of care.”

Half a dozen ShiftKey nurses and the two former corporate employees told Proof News and WIRED that many of the facilities that use ShiftKey have a history of poor quality of care and staffing issues.

One ShiftKey nurse recalled rats scurrying in the ceiling and roaches falling from lights at one nursing home.

Constance Hicks, a longtime certified nursing assistant in Connecticut, said that most nursing homes she worked at through ShiftKey were in terrible condition: no barrier cream, no soap, no supplies. Some places had no hot water. Not once in more than a year of picking up shifts through ShiftKey does she remember receiving any training at the homes.

In November 2023, while working a double shift at Cobalt Lodge Healthcare, Hicks discovered an elderly patient with their head and neck trapped in a bed rail, their forehead compressed against the metal, according to court records. She checked the patient’s vitals and, finding dangerously high blood pressure, called 911. Even though her shift had ended, Hicks stayed until emergency workers arrived.

Hicks said she documented everything and sent it to ShiftKey. She also tried reaching out to the company’s representatives but said no one responded. By the next day, her ShiftKey account was deactivated.

Hicks, who says the incident with the patient caused “a whole lot of psychological trauma,” tried to file a lawsuit against ShiftKey over the deactivation and other issues, but court records show the company successfully moved her case to private arbitration.

Cobalt Lodge Healthcare did not respond to a request for comment, and ShiftKey declined, citing ongoing litigation.

Regarding the quality of the facilities, Vitek said, “When professionals raise a concern, we encourage them to use the formal reporting channels, and remind them that they can choose whether they can accept future shifts there.”

Some lawmakers have begun scrutinizing platforms like ShiftKey, in part over concerns that it’s misclassifying its workers as independent contractors.

“It's not like they're coming in, bringing their own tools, fixing a pipe, and leaving,” says Emma Greenman, a Minnesota state representative, of gig nurses. “They are being managed by somebody.”

ShiftKey disputes that characterization. “ShiftKey, as a technology marketplace, does not employ healthcare professionals but connects them with healthcare facilities that have gaps in their schedule,” said Vitek, adding that the company works “tirelessly” to ensure its model complies with the law.

Greenman is working on a bill that she said would curb worker misclassification in Minnesota, including in gig nursing.

“What they’re doing is building business models to evade, break, and distort labor law for profit,” Greenman said.

There’s also the issue of whether to allow nursing homes to staff largely with gig workers. The year Lewis died, an analysis of staffing data submitted to CMS shows that nearly a third of the total nursing staff hours at Peachtree were performed by temporary workers.

Gary Poliakoff, one of the attorneys representing Lewis’ family, said that some weeks, the rate of temp workers including ShiftKey rose to as high as 50 percent of all nursing staff.

With little orientation, Poliakoff said, the model puts both patients—and workers—at a “great disadvantage.”

After the mistaken insulin injection, James Lewis said he got the call from Peachtree letting him know his mother was in the hospital. According to his deposition, he was getting ready to go to church to preach and planned to visit her later. He often went every day. They’d eat lunch together and watch The Price Is Right, but that day he was looking forward to spending some time outside. It was Mother’s Day.

When asked if he knew that Peachtree sometimes had temporary workers, he responded that he wasn’t aware.

“I don't know if it was a traveling nurse or what,” he said in the deposition. “But I know it wasn't a regular person.”

In her testimony, Kaye blamed understaffing for her insulin mix-up. She remembered working at Peachtree twice in November 2021 but went six months without returning because she thought it was a “shithole.”

“It was not a nice facility by any means,” Kaye said.

She testified she was already an hour late giving the insulin, having too much on her plate.

“I remember being not helped at all by administration, not knowing who anyone was,” said Kaye. “And pretty much being by myself.”

Updated 11/20/2026 at 8:52 am ET: WIRED updated the article to clarify a nurse’s use of a PICC line cited by a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in January.

#535. Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a new study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.

Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes. They detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many contained multiple toxins.

Mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

The investigation was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University. The researchers analyzed 212 products, including plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs). The selection covered foods commonly found on supermarket shelves, such as vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

Although the findings highlight how widespread these naturally occurring contaminants can be, the researchers also identified an important reassuring detail. Every product contained mycotoxin concentrations below recommended European Union guideline levels, which the team said reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

Why Plant-Based Foods Can Contain Fungal Toxins

Many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination. Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mold in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

Unlike bacteria or viruses, mycotoxins are chemical substances produced by certain fungi. Their presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mold, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe. The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

This distinction is especially important for people who eat plant-based products frequently. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter these substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Could Repeated Exposure Pose Health Risks?

While the concentrations detected in the UK products were below recommended EU guidelines, researchers say the potential effects of repeated exposure deserve closer attention.

Earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks. In other words, assessing a single product may not provide a complete picture of a person's overall dietary exposure.

Eating one of these products occasionally is unlikely to cause problems based on the levels reported. However, a diet that relies heavily or exclusively on plant-based foods could involve repeated exposure to mycotoxins from numerous ingredients and products. Researchers say understanding the combined effects is important for evaluating possible long-term health consequences.

The severity of mycotoxin exposure varies depending on the compounds involved and the amount consumed. At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

The new findings do not establish that the tested products cause these conditions. Instead, they provide information that scientists can use to estimate how much exposure consumers may receive through their diets and develop more accurate food safety risk assessments for the UK population.

Scientists Call for Better Monitoring of Plant-Based Ingredients

Andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, emphasized that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet. Mycology is the branch of biology devoted to studying fungi, including molds and yeasts.

"Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

However, a significant concern arises when new foods enter the market, as there are currently no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organizations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.

We are currently collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers."

The researchers are particularly interested in how food safety monitoring can keep pace with the growing range of plant-based products. Foods made from multiple ingredients present additional challenges because each component may introduce different contaminants, making overall exposure more difficult to assess.

Their work also underscores the importance of monitoring raw materials throughout the food production process. Identifying and controlling contamination before ingredients are combined into finished products could help manufacturers manage potential risks more effectively.

What the Findings Mean for Plant-Based Diets

The discovery of fungal toxins in all 212 products highlights the importance of studying dietary exposure across multiple foods, rather than evaluating each product in isolation.

For consumers, the results are not a reason to abandon vegan or vegetarian foods. The concentrations measured were below recommended EU guidelines, and the researchers stress that mycotoxins cannot be completely eliminated from the food supply.

Instead, the study points to the need for continued research into how different eating habits influence exposure, particularly among people who depend heavily on plant-based products. The University of Parma and Cranfield University are continuing their collaboration to investigate these dietary patterns, identify potentially vulnerable groups, and provide evidence that can inform future food safety policies.

The research, titled "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," was published in the journal Food Control.

The study was conducted as part of the European Union-funded Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03), Grant Agreement No 101079173.

Materials provided by Cranfield University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#534. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

#533. AO3 is down again, just days after returning from a 17-day outage

Updated on Nov. 19, 2026 at 1:56 p.m. ET / 4:46 p.m. PT — AO3 is now back online, having only been out of commission for less than a day this time. A few features remain disabled, such as downloading works in non-HTML formats, and OTW warns that users may experience an intentional delay in order to help it manage high traffic. Other than that, AO3 users should be able to get back to reading their favourite fanfics with minimal issues.

Archive of Our Own (AO3) is down again, just four days after the popular fanfiction platform came back online after a prolonged outage that left millions of readers scrambling for alternatives.

On Thursday, Nov. 19, users began reporting problems accessing the site, with outage-tracking website Downdetector showing a spike in reports beginning around 6:08 a.m. ET.

At 6:27 a.m. ET, AO3 confirmed the disruption, attributing it to preventative maintenance.

"AO3 is down for preventative maintenance," the platform wrote in an update. "We apologize for the inconvenience, and will provide updates when we have them."

The latest downtime comes after AO3 went offline on Oct. 29 for what became a 17-day maintenance period. At the time, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit behind AO3, warned that restoration could take two to four weeks, leaving fanfiction readers and writers without access to one of fandom's most important online archives.

AO3 finally returned on Nov. 15, though the site wasn't fully operational. User icons, imports from other sites, and downloads in formats other than HTML remained temporarily disabled as volunteers continued restoration efforts. The organization had previously warned that additional downtime could occur during the recovery process.

The prolonged outage prompted fans to look for other places to congregate online. Tumblr reported a 49 percent increase in new sign-ups during the first several days of AO3's absence, compared with the preceding two weeks, underscoring just how central the fanfiction archive has become to fandom communities.

But the disruption exposed growing tensions between fanfiction writers and readers. As readers scrambled to find copies of their favorite stories, some began circulating shared Google Drives containing downloaded works, prompting backlash from authors who hadn't consented to their stories being redistributed. The controversy sparked a larger conversation about ownership, consent, and the expectations that have developed between writers and readers in online fandom communities.

It's unclear whether Thursday's preventative maintenance is directly connected to the earlier outage or how long the latest disruption will last. AO3 has not provided an estimated restoration time.

For fanfiction readers who only just got their favorite archive back, it's another unwelcome plot twist.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

Previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

She's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

#531. Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

A new approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising new direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic

Over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

Despite these benefits, the medications have important limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

Berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

This process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second."

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

At the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

In mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an important benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

Perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is important for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the new research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

The compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

Other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

The Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

These receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

In mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," said study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively."

To understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

Surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an important part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

These medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

When the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.

In other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed

Despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

To help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology company called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

If the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an important addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

#530. U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.

"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles."

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response."

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

#529. Whos who in GTA 6? A guide to the characters (and memorable NPCs) weve met so far

Grand Theft Auto VI follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as a botched job drags them into a criminal conspiracy across Leonida, Rockstar's fictional version of Florida. But the most interesting details emerge from the people they encounter along the way — from smugglers in the Keys to rappers chasing stardom in Vice City.

We've compiled the characters we know about so far, including those Rockstar introduced before launch, and other GTA 6 NPCs who've appeared in reviews, gameplay clips, and our own playthroughs. We'll keep updating this list as we discover more.

Spoiler alert: This article contains plot and character details about the missions, side quests, and characters of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Jason Duval — A former soldier who works for drug runners in the Leonida Keys. He wants an easier life, but when a job goes wrong, he and Lucia get caught up in a much bigger criminal conspiracy. He's also a pretty good dancer.

Lucia Caminos — Jason's partner in crime. Her father taught her to fight growing up, and after a stint in Leonida Penitentiary, she's determined to build a better life for herself.

Brian Heder — A veteran smuggler who runs his operation out of a boatyard and lets Jason live rent-free in exchange for helping with jobs. His wife Lori is also involved.

Cal Hampton — Jason's friend and one of Brian's associates. He listens in on Coast Guard communications and has questions about why birds fly in formation.

Donnie — A member of Brian's crew who helps with drug and package runs.

Mandy — One of Brian's tenants. Jason goes to collect her overdue rent in the early mission "Pipework" and winds up helping with repairs. Their flirty exchange quickly made Mandy a launch-day fan favorite.

Shirley — Jason's neighbor in Key Lento. Her first request is a bottle of rum. Her second is a little more involved.

Peggy — Shirley's neighbor and the owner of the scooter Shirley wants Jason to steal. Peggy comes out to confront him when he tries to take it.

Dre'Quan Priest — An aspiring music mogul who books acts at Boobie’s club and signs Real Dimez.

Boobie Ike — The owner of the Jack of Hearts strip club and Dre'Quan's business partner at Only Raw Records.

Bae-Luxe and Roxy Rashad — High school friends who perform together as Real Dimez. They built a following with rap tracks and social media.

Raul Bautista — A seasoned bank robber always looking for people willing to take a chance on his next job.

Captain Aldo Méndez — A Vice City police officer who knows Jason and Lucia and takes part in a raid on Raymond's operation. A furry in a fox suit — While driving around as Lucia, a reviewer for Dexerto saw a police helicopter shine its spotlight on a man in a fox costume. They ended up helping him and his friends escape. Apparently, furries are where Leonida draws the line. (Seriously, there's apparently an anti-furry association in the game.)

A Hulk-like red giant — IShowSpeed ran into a towering red figure who tossed people and cars around and took on the police. The encounter reportedly ended with a hug before the giant leapt into the sky. Fans pointed out the plotline's connection with the villain in Captain America: Brave New World.

Animal rights protestors — During one part of the game, a group stops a truck taking a bear to a zoo. In a separate encounter, an animal rights protest leads to the player helping free a group of caged apes. GTA 6 gameplay prevents you from killing any protestors (yes, people tried).

Parrot smugglers at a liquor store — One reviewer for Fast Company came across a parrot-smuggling operation inside a liquor store. There's a side quest I wouldn’t have thought to look for, but GTA 6 is full of unexpected animal encounters.

Leonida's very own Bigfoot — Players on Reddit and X have been posting sightings of the Skunk Ape. In several clips, they find him near a dirt road with a deer carcass.
