#519. Service members offered time off to play GTA 6 — but theres a big catch

Is a four-day weekend of playing Grand Theft Auto VI worth two to six more years of military service? For 43 members of the U.S. Army's 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion in Georgia, the answer is indeed "yes."

Lt. Col. Ryan Hodgson offered 130 of his soldiers "a special 4-day pass" to play the game in exchange for reenlisting in the military — and one-third agreed to the terms, the Washington Post reports.

While servicemembers already receive numerous perks for reenlisting — from financial bonuses to special ceremonies to events with professional sports teams — Hodgson’s offer was a "cherry on top," Angel Tomko, a spokesperson for the Army’s 3rd Infantry Division, told the Post.

For soldiers already planning to reenlist, the offer is essentially a cheat code for an automatic 4-day pass.

Four days will just scratch the surface of GTA 6’s immersive world, which is a thinly veiled take on Florida. According to IGN (which is owned by Ziff Davis, Mashable’s parent company), its fastest player finished the game in 42 hours, while it took 115 hours for its slowest player to reach the end. Of course, the game has numerous secrets and side missions beyond the main objective of helping protagonists Jason and Lucia achieve their happy ending.

Meanwhile, critics and the public can't get enough GTA 6 — pre-orders alone have already topped $1 billion.

#518. YouTube bets on creator-led shows with a new slate

Streaming services and social platforms are giving internet creators more places to make their next hit show. Disney+ is adding videos from TikTok creators, Netflix is expanding its lineup of creator-led podcasts, and Instagram is testing videos up to 90 minutes long.

But when it comes to what Americans watch on TV, YouTube is still king. In August, it accounted for a record 15.8 percent of U.S. TV watch time, more than twice Netflix’s 7.7 percent and the biggest share of any company in the rankings.

This week, YouTube gave us a look at what some of its biggest creators are making, from shows that are already live to those coming in the months ahead. Here's what’s on the slate.

Emma Chamberlain — What Are You Waiting For? Emma Chamberlain hates waiting in line, which makes her an especially good person to ask New Yorkers why they do it. The 2026 Mashable 101 honoree visits some of the city's busiest lines and talks to the people in them about what’s worth giving up part of their day for. The line is just the starting point for a closer look at the fandoms and subcultures that bring people together in person. The series, produced by Amplify Pictures, premieres on Chamberlain's channel in early 2027.

Grace Reiter — Twilight (but better). After sending up Panem, Mashable 101 creator Grace Reiter is headed to Forks. The Saturday Night Live cast member and 2026 Mashable 101 honoree is directing and improvising her way through a Twilight parody, her second unscripted feature after The Hunger Games (but better), which drew more than 18 million views. The new one premieres Feb. 18 on Reiter's channel.

Aryna Sabalenka — Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered. What does wedding planning look like when most of the year is spent living out of a suitcase? Sabalenka's new docuseries follows the tennis champion from the tennis tour to dress fittings and brand meetings, including a project to design her own $250,000 diamond necklace. The show expands on her existing YouTube series, Aryna’s Arena, and premieres on her channel in spring 2027.

Wesley Wang — Response, Extract 14, and Absolute Cinema. If your group chat is always trying to solve the murder before the big reveal, Extract 14 will give you all something to work with. The six-episode mystery hides clues in found footage and offers $100,000 to the first viewer who cracks the case. Wang also has Response, a sci-fi horror short about park rangers who find something unsettling during a welfare check, and Absolute Cinema, which brings 10 aspiring filmmakers to New York for a weeklong boot camp. Viewers get the final say on who wins $100,000 to make their movie. Response is due in early 2027, with the other two projects following in the spring.

Nick DiGiovanni — Chef. Nick DiGiovanni went from MasterChef finalist to YouTube food star, building an audience with step-by-step recipes and stunts like making the world’s largest sushi roll. Now he's turning the camera on other chefs. His new channel, Chef, takes viewers inside Michelin-starred restaurants and street-food kitchens, with full-length episodes about the people behind the food and daily recipe Shorts filmed from the cook’s POV. The first two videos are already live: a visit to a pizza restaurant and a quick lesson in making butter chicken shawarma.

Morgan Jay — Music Therapy with Morgan Jay. Comedian, musician, and 2025 Mashable 101 cover star Morgan Jay is bringing his musical improv to the therapist's couch. In each episode, he plays therapist to a celebrity guest, and whatever comes up in their unscripted conversation becomes material for an original song they write and perform together. The first season’s guests include Mara Wilson, Yung Gravy, Ron Funches, and Josh Johnson. The series premiered Nov. 18 on Jay's YouTube channel.

The slate also includes Lilly Singh's Eligible Aunties, a dating series about older single women, and Track Star Tonight, a live music series from the team behind Jack Coyne's street quiz. Scott Evans heads to Lagos, Nigeria, for the Jan. 8 premiere of House Guest Vacay. Before then, Happy Hour with Ina Garten has a Thanksgiving special on Nov. 25, and Sam Eckholm goes behind the scenes with the Royal Air Force's Red Arrows on the Nov. 27 episode of Access Granted. New episodes of the docuseries Created with Jon Youshaei are also due this winter. That's a lot of new, original content!

YouTube has been working on two things a recurring show needs.

The first is a way for viewers to find the next episode. Creators can organize longer videos into seasons and episodes, and in September, YouTube announced a similar feature for Shorts, allowing viewers to watch them in order.

The second is a way to find sponsors. In March, YouTube introduced Creator Partnerships, which connects creators in YouTube Studio with marketers using Google’s ad tools. At the showcase, YouTube pointed to NYX's takeover of Mashable 101 star Brittany Broski's Royal Court and Expedia's partnership with another Mashable 101 creator, iShowSpeed.

One of the clearest examples is a show that aired for eight seasons on Netflix. Phil Rosenthal's Somebody Feed Phil will premiere its ninth season on his own YouTube channel this spring. United Airlines is the title sponsor and plans to carry the series on its in-flight screens, giving the show yet another place to reach viewers.

From YouTubers and TikTok stars to streamers and podcasters, Mashable talks to creators about how they built their platforms, the gear they swear by, and the trends they see coming next.

#517. FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop

The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."

Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

#516. Best Early Dyson Black Friday Vacuum Deals (2026)

I’m often asked if Dyson products are really worth the money. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy, and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson Black Friday deals have already started as of today. If you’re looking to pick up a new vacuum before your family comes over for Thanksgiving, here's the on-sale models I recommend.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals.

If you’re going to buy a Dyson vacuum on sale, you might as well go for one of the better ones. The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson’s most powerful stick vacuum, with 315 air-watts of power, some nice quality-of-life improvements in the body design, and an option to add the Submarine 2.0 mop head. I really liked this vacuum for the design upgrades and power level, but the price tag can be hard to stomach. It’s on sale fairly regularly, and there are a few different on-sale combos: The base vacuum is $180 off, bundling it with the Submarine head is $200 off, and the option with the charging Floor Dok is also $200 off. I love the Submarine head, but while I haven’t tested the vacuum with the Floor Dok yet, it’s the accessory I want most—having your cordless vacuum fully charged whenever you want it, and somewhere to store it, is really handy.

If you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599), and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). It's a great all-around vacuum, and this bundle option gets you great extra attachments.

The PencilVac is incredibly handy and compact, and great if you're trying to do quick pickups daily on hard floors. You won't want it if you have any kind of rug or carpet, since it's only designed for hard flooring, but I did find it incredibly easy to grab and use for constant litter trails in my house. It's incredibly lightweight and a great fit for anyone with mobility or strength concerns. If these features speak to you, this is a great time to buy, as it's already on sale.

This wet floor cleaner is often on sale for around $400, so it's not a huge surprise to see this deal ahead of Black Friday. The Dyson Clean+Wash is primarily a wet floor cleaner, but it can do dry cleans, too, and does not use a filter you inevitably need to keep clean. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck noticed no weird smells in three months of use. It's similar to the Dyson WashG1, with a self-propelled design that makes it easy to push around the room, and it does a good job scrubbing floors clean. Keep in mind that it's not great for dry debris, since its just rolling, not sucking.

The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year and is one of my favorite robot vacuums from the brand. That's including the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m currently testing, which hasn't blown me away as a better investment. (It actually failed my corner test completely, which vacuums in that price range should not do.)

The Spot+Scrub Ai is much lower priced, and despite some dubious AI feature claims, it does a good job cleaning autonomously. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what I saw during Prime Day.

#515. Microsoft CEO explains reason behind the 60,000 buyouts (its AI, of course)

Last month, Microsoft asked as many as 60,000 employees to voluntarily leave their jobs with buyout offers. This week, CEO Satya Nadella took some time to explain why.

In a talk with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the New York Times' DealBook Summit in New York City (as reported by TechCrunch), Nadella addressed the buyout offer that made headlines in October. As we reported at the time, the buyouts came amidst a huge amount of AI investment at Microsoft and industry-wide AI layoffs. And in his comments at the summit, Nadella made it explicitly clear that the company reorganization was necessary because of AI.

You can listen to the CEO's full comments at about 27:20 in the New York Times' YouTube video of the interview:

According to Nadella, it's not necessarily about directly replacing humans with AI in a one-to-one fashion. However, that may not be comforting to workers asked to leave their jobs, if only voluntarily. “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” Nadella said.

Like many tech leaders, Nadella believes the future of development at Microsoft and beyond involves humans managing a team of AI agents, an approach that many Big Tech companies have already adopted. For example, the team behind the Microsoft 365 AI agent Cowork consists of only 11 human beings who, in Nadella's words, "build a software factory that builds the product" rather than writing the product code themselves.

Rather than simply laying off workers, Nadella said the buyouts were intended to give workers some measure of control over their future at Microsoft.

By opting for buyouts, the CEO said that he wanted “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," per TechCrunch.

#514. Fiona the hippo, one of the internets most beloved animal icons, has died

Fiona, the beloved Cincinnati Zoo hippo who became an internet sensation after surviving a premature birth in 2017, has died at age 9. The zoo announced Thursday that Fiona died after accidentally swallowing a knit hat that fell into her enclosure earlier this month, despite days of intensive veterinary care.

Her death has prompted an outpouring of grief online from fans who watched her grow from a vulnerable 29-pound newborn into one of the internet's most recognizable animal celebrities.

Born six weeks premature, Fiona became a viral sensation as the Cincinnati Zoo documented her unlikely survival on social media. Millions followed her progress, celebrating everything from her first steps to her swimming lessons. Nearly a decade later, she remained a beloved fixture of internet culture, inspiring memes, merchandise, and a devoted online following.

Nearly a decade later, the internet is mourning her loss. The Cincinnati Zoo confirmed her death in a heartbreaking statement, explaining that its veterinary team had spent days attempting to help Fiona pass the foreign object. Despite round-the-clock care and multiple treatments, her condition deteriorated.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement, as reported by the BBC. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

According to the zoo, the hat entered Fiona's habitat in a freak accident involving a visitor and a ceiling fan. The zoo consulted veterinary and medical specialists, but surgery was not considered a viable option for the full-grown hippo.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," Jenike said. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore."

Long before the internet fell in love with Moo Deng, there was Fiona.

When Fiona arrived on Jan. 24, 2017, she was the smallest premature hippo known to survive in human care. Unable to stand long enough to nurse from her mother, Bibi, she required intensive care from zoo staff, who worked alongside specialists from Cincinnati Children's Hospital to keep her alive.

Her recovery quickly became an online phenomenon. Through photos, videos, and regular updates from the Cincinnati Zoo, fans followed Fiona's earliest milestones, from learning to swim to growing strong enough to reunite with her family. The hashtag #TeamFiona became a rallying cry for people who had never visited Cincinnati but nevertheless felt invested in the little hippo's survival.

She eventually inspired children's books, merchandise, memes, and even an ice cream flavor. Her birthday became an occasion for celebration, and visitors traveled from around the world to see her in person.

For the past nine years, Fiona has been a familiar presence in people's social media feeds, an unlikely celebrity whose fans have watched her grow from a vulnerable newborn into a playful, 2,000-pound hippo.

And unlike so many fleeting internet sensations, Fiona never really disappeared from the public's affection.

News of Fiona's death prompted an outpouring of grief across social media Thursday, with longtime fans sharing memories, photographs, and tributes to the hippo who had become a symbol of resilience.

For many, the circumstances of her death made the news especially difficult to process. Social media users expressed anger that an accidentally discarded object could have such devastating consequences, while others urged compassion and discouraged directing harassment toward the family involved.

The loss also resonated with Cincinnati residents, for whom Fiona had become something of an unofficial mascot. Her unlikely survival story was woven into the city's identity, and her life had been celebrated by generations of zoo visitors.

"Fiona was such a gift," Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard said in a statement. "I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life."

For an animal whose earliest days were shared with the world, her death feels unusually personal. Millions of people watched her learn to swim, celebrated her birthdays, and cheered as she grew into a healthy adult. They knew her story because they had been following it almost from the beginning.

The internet helped make Fiona famous. But it was her unlikely survival — and the joy she brought people along the way — that made her unforgettable.

#512. Dont worry, Artificials unsettling AI poster was actually made by a human

NEON has released a new poster for Luca Guadagnino's upcoming OpenAI film Artificial, and the visual is peak uncanny valley.

The illustrated poster centers on Andrew Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who stands in a redwood forest overlooking San Francisco Bay. He holds out a hand, inviting us into an unknown future.

For anyone who's ever wanted to go hiking with Garfield, the image seems like a dream come true. But stare at the poster for more than one second, and your brain starts to reject everything that's in front of it. Why does that redwood have a face? Why is a grassy hill glitching into a tunnel? Why does Altman look like he's about to call me "Spider Monkey" and take me on a piggyback ride through the woods, Edward Cullen-style?

Most importantly: Why does everything carry the discomforting sheen of AI? Could NEON have missed the point of Artificial's cautionary tale entirely and made promotional materials using AI?

Don't panic. A line of text alongside the bottom right edge of the poster affirms that the artwork was made by humans. To back that affirmation up, NEON also released a video of the poster being digitally illustrated, tagging creative agency Gravillis Inc. and artist Mike Thompson.

Comments under NEON's initial post of the poster appreciated the clever AI-adjacent marketing tactic.

"Chefs kiss on the poster which was made by an artist satirizing the AI aesthetic we all know and (should) hate," one user wrote.

"Poster meant to look like AI, but still has the humanity of an artist, so it’s still pretty to look at," wrote another.

If you were still somehow on the fence about whether Artificial would be pro- or anti-AI, look no further than the poster's background, which shows the Golden Gate Bridge partially submerged. Whatever future Garfield's Altman wants to bring us into, it's clearly calamitous.

#511. Booking Holdings creates new enterprise division as AI reshapes travel planning

Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a new division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips.

The new enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers.

"We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

He said existing partners will find new and better products, which will also help grow the partner base.

The move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The company says partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution.

The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the company.

Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy launched in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings.

From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the company said in 2024.

In 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year.

Morgenshtern declined to say how much the new division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he said the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion.

Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel.

Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the new starting point for planning and reservations.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said on the company’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and plan Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book.

“Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he said, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them.

Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the company's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it said.

"I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern said, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

#510. France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

#507. Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself

After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”

Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.)

Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.)

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

“Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz says. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”

Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the company offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest company in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.

Google gives users the ability to freely choose which apps Gemini has access to, alongside the ability to watch the process as it unfolds, in case something goes wrong. So, you can pause Gemini if it's doing something you don't like, and approve decisions before they're made. #504. Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.

It’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

But if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit quickly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

But what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo says in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

As Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

Voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.)

For Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally launched to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really big gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

Newton’s second law of motion says that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

Let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

Not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

It’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.

#503. GTA 6 inspires DoorDash, UberEats, Grubhub discount codes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) was finally released into the wild on Nov. 19, unveiling the beloved video game franchise's first title in 13 years. The highly anticipated game even inspired eager fans to take time off work in favor of immersing themselves in GTA 6, reveling in everything from crashing planes to home renovation in-game.

Yet while our virtual avatars engage in miscellaneous violent crimes, our physical bodies still require sustenance. Food delivery apps such as Uber Eats, DoorDash, and Grubhub have thus jumped on the GTA 6 hype, offering discount codes to those too locked in to their marathon gaming session to cook.

DoorDash's GTA 6 discounts are the most limited in terms of food options, offering $6 off Cheesecake Factory orders of $20 or more. Customers just need to enter the discount code CAKEGTA6 when placing their DoorDash order, with the offer only available on Nov. 19.

The company is also offering $15 off orders of $20 or more from Wendy's with codes given out on the Wendy's Twitch stream until 9 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. PT (check the scrolling bar at the top of the screen). However, these DoorDash codes are limited to the first 100 customers, and only valid for 30 minutes after they're released.

Uber Eats' discount code ONAMISSION will save users $10 off an order of $20 or more, and isn't restricted to a specific restaurant. Uber Eats has indicated this code is specifically for GTA 6's launch day, so if you're interested you should redeem it sooner rather than later.

Grubhub's discount code OUTOFOFFICE offered $10 off orders over $10, and was active from 9 a.m. ET / 6 a.m. PT on GTA 6 launch day. Unfortunately, it was limited to the first 1,000 customers, with some people reporting that they were unable to use the code within minutes of the promotion being posted. Less than an hour and a half later, Grubhub confirmed that its GTA 6-inspired discount code had been exhausted.

Food delivery apps have apparently received an influx of orders surrounding GTA 6's launch. The New York Times reports that DoorDash's energy drink sales spiked by over 20 percent on Wednesday, when many Grand Theft Auto fans stayed up for the game's midnight launch. DoorDash's Wednesday night sales were reportedly up by double digits in multiple U.S. states, while UberEats' overnight sales increased by 30 percent in Miami (the inspiration behind GTA 6's Vice City).

The next few days may be busy for food delivery workers, with gamers expected to spend hours exploring GTA 6. As such, remember to be patient and tip well. No doubt they'd rather be playing as well.

#501. Wars final verdict explained by Dominic West and Sienna Miller

After a full season of cutthroat legal proceedings, War's central divorce trial between actor Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) has reached its final verdict. The winner? No one. But the loser? Also no one.

That's because, after some eleventh-hour heroics from mole Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) and honeypot Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), Carla and Morgan reach their own settlement, independent of their lawyers and the judge. Following their decision, Carla will receive 50 percent of Zephyr's shares and monthly payments from Morgan until he retires. Carla and Morgan will share custody of Carla's son, Gabe (Aran Murphy). In short, it's basically what Carla had been asking for this whole time, and what the pair could have achieved without going to court.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Their decision stems from hearing Flora read Morgan's conciliatory letter to Carla, which St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) tried to dispose of, aloud in court. For Carla and Morgan, the letter is a reminder of the good in their relationship, something they sorely needed to recall after months of highly public mud-slinging.

"It tied itself up with humanity and kindness, and that was unexpected for me when I was reading it," Miller told Mashable in a junket interview alongside West. "I think the moral of that being that had these two people dropped their ego and their pride and nasty covetousness, if they'd let all of that go, they could have probably resolved this without the hideous experience of taking each other to court."

"It felt like a spectacular waste of $10 million on lawyers' fees," West joked.

For series creator George Kay, there was never a version of War Season 1 where the court ruled in favor of one side or the other.

"In the majority of these big divorces, the real winners are the lawyers, and so we wanted to take that agency away from the justice system and put it back in the hands of [Carla and Morgan]," Kay told Mashable in a junket interview. "So, it was always going to be down to them to work it out, which is the big expensive irony of what they've been through."

By the end of Season 1, Carla and Morgan have found what seems to be an affectionate alliance. Even though Carla now has the Zephyr shares she asked for, she won't be using them against Morgan to trigger the sale to Michael Ancker (David Menkin), as Zephyr CEO Gillian Pope (Angel Coulby) wanted. Instead, Gillian is being ousted, as it turns out she leaked the security footage of Flora leaving Morgan's hotel room to the press.

In War's final scene between Carla and Morgan, the pair stand, at peace, on a Normandy beach by their cottage.

"I'll always love you," Morgan tells Carla.

As it seems that the pair is about to go their separate ways, Carla calls Morgan back up to the cottage for a hot chocolate with Gabe. It's proof that their life as a pairing isn't over. It's just taken a different shape. And maybe thanks to that, both Carla and Morgan "won" in the trial after all.

"The end of a divorce, it's not like someone's dead," West said. "You either never speak to each other again, run screaming through the streets, or you realize actually why you love the person in the first place. I think that's what happens to Morgan in the end."

"We described this divorce at the world's most expensive couples therapy, because it's only by going through everything that they've been through, hearing what the other one thinks via their lawyers, emotionally reengaging with everything they've had in their relationship, that by the end they realize what an amazing thing they have, and so we leave them okay," Kay said. "They're divorced, technically, but actually they're much better parents and they're much closer emotionally, and that was always a North Star for us."

The sweet ending for Morgan and Carla is at odds with the rest of War's bloodthirsty, win-at-any-cost tone. But for Kay, that was intentional.

"We didn't want it to be bleak or dark," Kay said of the ending. "We wanted it to be redemptive."

#499. Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market

Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.

The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program."

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

#497. Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire

Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing."

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges."

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

#496. 21 Best Home Entertainment Gifts (2026): TVs, Lights, and More

Maybe I'm just a hermit (or maybe everything in NYC is too damned expensive), but some of the most fun I've had in recent memory hasn't been going out. It's been in homes, whether it's for family movie night or for catching up with friends over drinks.

Upgrading your home entertainment setup is more than just buying a new TV or projector. Pair it with a new espresso machine or pizza oven, and you'll have the recipe for a go-to hosting location for get-togethers of all types. Below are some of the best pieces of WIRED-tested gear to upgrade any home entertainment setup, for yourself or for someone who would be over the moon unboxing a new set of speakers.

Looking for more gifting inspiration? Check out our guides to the Best Gifts for Mom, Best Gifts for Friends, Best Techie Gifts, and Best Gifts for Outdoorsy Folks.

Quite simply the best OLED TV we've tested, the Samsung S95H is bright, clear, and colorful, with outstanding picture quality and AI optimizations that eke out as much detail as possible. It's also a looker, with a silver bezel around the screen that gives the illusion of a metal picture frame. It comes in sizes ranging from 55 inches to 83 inches.

It's the best soundbar you can get, as well as the best all-in-one home theater audio solution. Everything from the unboxing down to the texture of the bar itself is premium with the Sonos Arc Ultra. And most importantly, its sound is stunning, especially considering it's slim footprint.

Looking to replicate the movie-going experience? The LG Sound Suite H7 is a great soundbar that comes in plenty of bundles with other LG subwoofers and wireless speakers. My favorite is the Immersive Suite 5 Pro bundle, which comes with the soundbar, a subwoofer, and two wireless speakers.

A premium home theater projector can make movies look bigger and better than even some of the best TVs. This Leica Cine Play 1 is a perfect example. Colors pop with vivid clarity, and you can project a 65- to 300-inch image—big enough for even the largest of parties.

Bookshelf speakers have a certain je ne sais quoi about them that other speakers can only dream of. The KEF LSX II have that classy bookshelf look with seriously modern smarts inside. You can plug these into your TV, turntable, and additional subwoofers, or forego cables entirely and use them via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

Want a 100-inch TV that will truly impress? You need an RGB TV like the LG Micro RGB Evo above. RGB is the latest innovation to hit TV screens, with vibrant and bold colors you'd be hard-pressed to find elsewhere.

Light can add a new level of immersion to any home theater. The Nanoleaf 4D Kit did just that for WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell. “I watched Return of the King with 4D lighting, and I never want to go back.”

This weighted blanket comes recommended by WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins, and it makes any movie night instantly cozy, regardless of the weather. It's woven from 100 percent cotton and comes in four different weight options, ranging from 10 to 25 pounds.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, this fluffy, stretchy blanket is like being surrounded by a cloud, says Higgins. “I promise this gift will be fought over at the next movie night.”

Entertainment equipment doesn't have to be drab blocks of black or white. The Audioengine Color of the Year kit comes with a turntable, bookshelf speakers, and a subwoofer, all in matching bright yellow. It's a cinch to set up and a great way to add music and color to any room.

Entertainment isn't restricted to the TV room. A great turntable makes any room a space for gathering and enjoying some music. This one from Fluance is one of our favorites, with a warm, subtle design and premium components.

Pair the RT81+ turntable with a matching set of these Fluance bookshelf speakers and you've got a setup that can deliver incredible clarity for everything, including vinyl and Bluetooth streaming.

An instant camera equals instant party favors—they've certainly been used at basically every wedding I've been to recently. Whether you're hosting a monthly movie night or a big NFL watch party, this instant camera is chic and can instantly print out photos for anyone to take home.

Elegant. Precise. Beautiful. Functional. We love this electric kettle for all these reasons. Why for home entertainment? Well, a lot of people I host prefer tea to beer, especially as winter approaches.

This sleek semiautomatic espresso machine is quite showy in person. It has a dual boiler, meaning you can froth milk as you're pulling a shot, and it comes with plenty of accessories.

Want a drink with your entertainment? This toolkit elevates the mixing experience, with a diamond-cut mixing glass, julep strainer, stainless steel jigger, and stainless steel teardrop bar spoon. All pieces are made in Japan and sourced by Umami Mart, an independently owned small business in Oakland, California.

Take your movie literally anywhere with this compact portable projector. It has a built-in stand, which is also how you adjust the projector angle. The stand also makes it easy to store anywhere in the house. The battery won't last through a whole movie, so it's better for shorter TV shows or paired with a backup portable power station.

If you have an outlet outside (or a portable power station), the Nebula X1 is one of the best compact projectors for entertainment anywhere. It's bright, colorful, and displays an image up to 200 inches. Plus, you can bundle it with wireless speakers or karaoke mics.

The Sonos Move 2 is the most-used speaker in my apartment because it is so versatile. Leave it docked indoors and you have a smart, Wi-Fi connected home speaker for music. Take it outdoors, and you have a powerful, durable Bluetooth speaker with IP56 dust and water resistance. Pair two with a Sonos soundbar, and you have an impromptu surround sound experience.

An outdoor pizza oven is a show all on its own, but pair it with an outdoor projector, and you've got entertainment (and food) for everyone. The Karu 2 is the best one we've tested.

String lights aren't just for holidays anymore. Think of them more like great outdoor lights that can go anywhere: around a big tree, along a fence line, wherever.

#494. NYT Strands hints, answers for November 20, 2026

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you're always in a pickle.

Strands, the New York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

If you're feeling stuck or just don't have 10 or more minutes to figure out today's puzzle, we've got all the NYT Strands hints for today's puzzle you need to progress at your preferred pace.

Today's NYT Strands spangram is vertical.
